question: Why does measuring one entangled electron instantly affect the other, light-years away?
answer: After two electrons interact, they no longer have separate wave functions; one wave function describes both. Measuring either electron collapses that whole wave function, so the other is set at the same instant, however far away.
move: Entangled means one wave function for two particles: collapse it anywhere, it collapses everywhere.

web.label: Wave functions as clouds of dots: electrons A and B, each in its own cloud. A tap: they meet, the clouds become one, and they fly apart with that one cloud stretched light-years between them. A tap on A measures it: the whole cloud collapses at once, A is up and B down in that instant, while light from A is still on its way. Asks why measuring one entangled electron affects the other.

source: Veritasium, “Why Parallel Universes Are Probably Real” (YouTube, 2020)
